Dozens have objected to the plans, which would see a solar farm built next to a popular fishing site

The proposed solar farm would be built in the north west of Chertsey, in the Twynersh Meadows (Image: Chertsey Bridge)(Image: Matt\_Gibson / Getty Images)
Plans for a 100-panel solar farm near a Surrey town and just off the M25 have been met with strong opposition from residents and local organisations.
It would "destroy the heritage" of our beautiful town" Chertsey residents have said in response to proposals for a large solar farm just off Thorpe Road in the northwest of the town.
Initial plans were submitted by developers Roger Mugford and Pegasus Group back in 2024 with residents launching a petition to fight it in October that year. To date, the petition has over 800 signatures.
In June 2025, a full planning application for the project was submitted. This has since received dozens of comments of objection from the community, with some warning that the area is "frequently underwater" due to flooding.
An image of the Littleton Solar Project in Evesham, Worcestershire. The proposed solar farm in Chertsey could look similar, should it be approved by planning officers
An image of the Littleton Solar Project in Evesham, Worcestershire. The proposed solar farm in Chertsey could look similar, should it be approved by planning officers(Image: TfL)
The proposals would see around 100 solar panels, a battery energy storage facility, EV chargers and an 'Eco Hub' fit with a café and car park built on land north of St Ann's Road and west of Thorpe Road in Chertsey, known as the Twynersh Meadows.
This site is based on the other side of Thorpe Road to the Chertsey Lake and flood plains, as well as just east of St Ann's Hill Park and Nature Trail with the M25 and M3 also both just minutes drive away.
Runnymede Borough Council is set to decide whether to approve or reject the application in the coming months, with its public consultation period ending in March.
The solar farm planning application pertains to the area highlighted in yellow, just off Thorpe Road
The solar farm planning application pertains to the area highlighted in yellow, just off Thorpe Road(Image: Google)
During the consultation, the plans were met with a fierce response, with one resident who was made aware of the proposals through social media saying:
"I object because this is farmland which is also known for flooding each year. Why destroy the heritage of our beautiful town Chertsey by putting in solar panels and EV chargers when they could be placed elsewhere? It will be an eye sore.
"The town is already becoming over populated as it is and this will make it worse. Leave it as land how it currently is, we don’t need anymore built up areas, our town can’t cope as it is."
One commenter highlighted the condition of the land, saying: "I am amazed this has even been considered, after all the rain we’ve had the end of last year this land is still waterlogged and you are thinking of placing solar panels battery charging on it?
"The surrounding roads are clogged as it is we don’t need more traffic, more cars near a school. The water in this field runs off into the school why increase the risk?
"Green belt land used for grazing should not be used for the convenience of car drivers. Surely some common sense can be applied? Water and electricity do not mix. Cars and children do not mix."
An image of the site proposed for the solar farm development taken from Thorpe Road on Google Street View
An image of the site proposed for the solar farm development taken from Thorpe Road on Google Street View(Image: Google )
Another person who claimed to work in Thorpe and use nearby roads often took to the comments to say: "I work in Thorpe and drive past this road and it is often flooded in winter, sometimes onto the road, this would make it worse and dangerous as a variety fast road.
"This seems pointless to me as charging points can be out anywhere in local car parks. More green belt and not to mention historical areas do not need to be destroyed for something that has a short lifespan and won’t really benefit the people of Chertsey at all. Trees are needed more than this is. They contribute to our health."
"This (land) should be preserved for the environmental, historical and local preservation of natural, beautiful green space." The comment concluded.
The Chertsey Society also expressed its objection to the plans, with a spokesperson for the organisation saying: "The Chertsey Society welcomes car charging points in the district, but notes with concern the placement of one such sensitive position.
"Twynersh Meadows is a green entry into the town and should be preserved as such a small but important portion of England’s green and pleasant land."

Alan Wood & Partners were appointed to deliver civil engineering design services for a new 360MW Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and associated 400kV substation in Staythorpe, Nottinghamshire (currently under construction). Working in collaboration with Mitie Power & Grid, the project required a resilient design to meet operational demands and environmental challenges. Scope of Work
• Flood Compensation Storage Modelling: Developed to offset floodplain impacts and maintain compliance with regulatory requirements.  
• Drainage Design: Engineered surface water drainage networks to manage runoff effectively and prevent localised flooding.  
• Earthworks & Platform Design: Formation of BESS and substation platforms, optimised for cost-effective earthworks while meeting key flood risk requirements.
Challenges
• Designing for flood resilience while maintaining cost efficiency.  
• Managing settlement risks for heavy battery and transformer installations.  
• Integrating access and drainage solutions within a constrained site layout.
The project delivered a robust, flood-resilient platform and infrastructure capable of supporting a 360MW energy storage facility, ensuring compliance with standards and long-term operational reliability
